formulaCard.title: Net Pay Formula

explanation: A [[kw:payroll register]] lists each employee’s gross pay, deductions, and net pay for a pay period.
[[kw:Net pay]] (take‑home pay) = Gross Pay – Total Deductions.
Deductions include federal income tax (FIT), state income tax (SIT), Social Security (FICA‑OASDI), Medicare (FICA‑HI), and voluntary deductions (health insurance, retirement).
[[imp:Gross pay is before deductions; net pay is what the employee actually receives.]]
The payroll register is the source document for recording payroll in the accounting system.

discoveryHook.scenario: Ramon Valdez earned $650.25 gross pay, but his paycheck is only $520.37. The missing $129.88 went to taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and other deductions. The [[kw:payroll register]] records all these calculations and shows how gross pay becomes net pay (take‑home pay).

blocks.title: 2. FICA Taxes: Social Security & Medicare

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The Social Security wage cap changes most years. [[imp:Always use the current year's cap and rates when calculating FICA.]]

formulaCard.title: FICA Tax Withholding
notes: Social Security tax applies only up to the annual wage base.
Medicare has no cap; additional 0.9% applies to high incomes.
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Social Security Tax} = \text{Gross Pay} \times 0.062$$ $$\text{Medicare Tax} = \text{Gross Pay} \times 0.0145$$ $$\text{Total FICA} = \text{SS} + \text{Medicare}$$

explanation: [[kw:FICA]] consists of two parts: Social Security (OASDI) and Medicare (HI).
Social Security tax rate = 6.2% on the first $168,600 (2024 cap; annually adjusted) of wages. Above the cap, no Social Security tax is withheld.
Medicare tax rate = 1.45% on all wages, with no cap. High earners may pay an additional 0.9% above a threshold.
Both taxes are deducted from the employee's gross pay; the employer matches these amounts.
[[imp:FICA taxes are mandatory; they fund benefits for retirees, disabled workers, and Medicare recipients.]]

visuals.caption: Rates are current as of tax year 2024; check for annual updates.
visuals.title: FICA Tax Breakdown

blocks.title: 3. Federal and State Income Tax

visuals.caption: Allowances reduce taxable wages for withholding purposes. (Illustrative values only.)
visuals.title: Sample Federal Tax Withholding (Weekly, Single, 2024)

explanation: [[kw:Federal Income Tax (FIT)]] is withheld according to IRS tax tables, using the employee's gross pay, pay frequency, and W‑4 allowances.
[[kw:State Income Tax (SIT)]] varies by state; some states have a flat rate, others a graduated scale, and a few have no state income tax.
Employers use the employee's W‑4 to determine the number of allowances, which affect the withholding amount.
FIT and SIT are not flat percentages of gross pay; they are progressive and depend on earnings.
[[imp:Higher allowances on W‑4 mean less tax withheld from each paycheck.]]

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{FIT} = \text{Wage Bracket Method using IRS Circular E}$$
formulaCard.title: Income Tax Withholding
notes: Exact withholding requires current tax tables or percentage method.
SIT is calculated using state‑specific formulas.

teacherCues: Show how to use tax tables to find FIT based on earnings and W-4 allowances.
Explain that state income tax varies by state; some states have none.

blocks.title: 4. Voluntary Deductions & Net Pay

visuals.title: Deductions from Gross Pay
visuals.caption: Both mandatory and voluntary deductions reduce take‑home pay.

explanation: [[kw:Voluntary deductions]] are amounts employees choose to have withheld, such as health insurance, retirement contributions, and union dues.
Some voluntary deductions are pre‑tax (e.g., 401(k), health premiums) and reduce taxable wages for federal and state income tax.
After all mandatory taxes (FICA, FIT, SIT) and voluntary deductions are subtracted, the remainder is [[kw:net pay]].
Net pay = Gross Pay – (Mandatory Taxes + Voluntary Deductions).
[[imp:Pre‑tax deductions lower your taxable income now but are taxed later when withdrawn (retirement).]]

notes: Pre‑tax deductions are subtracted before calculating FIT and SIT.
Post‑tax deductions (like Roth 401(k)) are taken from net pay after taxes.
formulaCard.title: Net Pay with All Deductions

discoveryHook.scenario: Ramon chose to contribute $19.63 to his 401(k) and pay $10.00 for dental insurance. These [[kw:voluntary deductions]] come out of his gross pay after mandatory taxes, leaving his final net pay. Pre‑tax deductions (like 401(k)) also lower his current taxable income.

blocks.title: 5. Employer’s Payroll Taxes: FUTA & SUTA
teacherCues: Explain that employers pay payroll taxes in addition to withholding employee taxes.
List the two unemployment taxes: FUTA (federal) and SUTA (state).

explanation: [[kw:FUTA]]: federal unemployment tax, currently 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages. Employers may receive a credit of up to 5.4% for paying state unemployment taxes, resulting in a net FUTA rate of 0.6%.
[[kw:SUTA]]: state unemployment tax, rates and wage bases vary by state. Often the wage base is higher than $7,000.
Both taxes are paid only by the employer; they are not deducted from employees.
[[imp:Employer payroll taxes are a significant additional cost of having employees.]]
Also, employers must match the employee's FICA contributions (equal amounts).

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{FICA matching} = (\text{SS} \times 2) + (\text{Med.} \times 2)$$ $$\text{FUTA} = \text{Taxable Wages (up to 7,000)} \times 0.006$$ $$\text{SUTA} = \text{Taxable Wages (state base)} \times \text{State Rate}$$
formulaCard.title: Employer Payroll Tax Expense
notes: SS and Medicare matching: employer pays the same as employee.
FUTA rate often reduced to 0.6% if SUTA is paid.

visuals.title: Employer Payroll Taxes (per employee)
visuals.caption: Employer costs add roughly 7.65% (FICA) plus unemployment taxes to each employee's wages.
